Signing Real Tokens in Integration Tests →

Testing Middleware Directly

authenticate.js and authorize.js get the same fake-req/next treatment Lesson 3 gave validate.js — with one real token thrown in.

authenticate.js and authorize.js are both plain functions that read a fake-able req and call a fake-able next — exactly the shape Lesson 3's validate.middleware.test.js already established a pattern for, and both new suites reuse it directly:

// Figure 4.16: a fake req, a real signed token (tests/unit/authenticate.middleware.test.js, excerpt)
const fakeReq = (authorizationHeader) => ({
  get: (name) => (name === 'Authorization' ? authorizationHeader : undefined),
});

it('attaches req.user from a valid Bearer token', () => {
  const token = signToken({ sub: 5, role: 'agent' });
  const req = fakeReq(`Bearer ${token}`);
  const next = jest.fn();

  authenticate(req, {}, next);

  expect(req.user).toEqual({ id: 5, role: 'agent' });
  expect(next).toHaveBeenCalledWith();
});

fakeReq only needs to satisfy the one thing authenticate.js actually calls on req — req.get('Authorization') — so a plain object with a get method is a complete enough stand-in for a real Express request. The token itself is real, though, produced by the actual signToken (this lesson's JWT topic) rather than some hand-written fake string — there'd be little point testing authenticate against a token shaped nothing like one verifyToken would ever actually receive.

authorize.middleware.test.js is simpler still: it never touches tokens at all, just calls authorize('agent', 'admin')(req, {}, next) against a plain { user: { id, role } } object and checks whether next was called cleanly or with a 403 — proof that authorize itself needs nothing more than req.user already being set, exactly as designed (the role-based- authorization topic).
